# Car or e-bike for the daily commute?

*Test fixture written for this repo. The numbers are illustrative.*

For short trips, an electric bike can replace many car journeys. Both turn energy into distance, but they do it very differently.

A typical petrol car uses about 7 litres of fuel per 100 kilometres. Burning a litre of petrol releases about 2.3 kilograms of carbon dioxide, so each kilometre adds about 160 grams of CO2. Petrol costs around $1.90 a litre.

An e-bike uses roughly 1 kilowatt hour of electricity for every 100 kilometres: about one hundredth of the energy. On an average grid, a kilowatt hour causes about 0.5 kilograms of CO2, so an e-bike kilometre causes about 5 grams. A kilowatt hour costs around 30 cents.

For a 10 kilometre commute each way, five days a week, 46 weeks a year, the car burns about 320 litres of petrol a year and emits about 740 kilograms of CO2. The e-bike uses about 46 kilowatt hours.

People often think the e-bike's battery and charging cancel out most of the gain. They don't: even counting the electricity, the e-bike emits a few percent of the car's CO2 for the same trip.

An e-bike costs around $2,500 and needs servicing. It does not suit every trip: heavy loads, bad weather and long distances still favour the car. Many households keep the car and use the e-bike for most commutes.
